title: Experimental Realization of a C-Shunt Flux-Qubit Coupler for Controlled-Z Gates between Transmons
authors: Weiping Yuan, Silu Zhao, Li Li, Chenglin Deng, Zhenghe Liu, Yu Liu, Tianming Li, Mingchuan Wang, Bingjie Chen, Guihan Liang, Jiacheng Song, Jinming Guo, Shuaili Wang, Mingxuan Zhou, Xiaohui Song, Kai Xu, Heng Fan, Zhongcheng Xiang, Dongning Zheng
abstract: Fast entangling gates and low-interaction idling require distinct operating conditions in superconducting quantum processors. We experimentally realize a transmon-C-shunt-transmon (TCT) device in which a flux-tunable, three-junction capacitively shunted flux-qubit coupler connects two transmon data qubits. The C-shunt coupler provides a flux-tunable, positively anharmonic spectrum for tailoring the interactions between the data qubits. Conditional Ramsey and swap measurements identify an idle region with near-zero residual ZZ interaction strength and suppressed transverse exchange. At this bias, simultaneous single-qubit interleaved randomized benchmarking yields X-gate fldelities above 99.7%, consistent with individual operation. A 45 ns nonadiabatic controlled-Z (CZ) gate achieves an interleaved randomized benchmarking fldelity estimate of 99.23(15)%. Numerical simulations identify coupler energy relaxation as an important limitation on CZ-gate fldelity and indicate that extending the coupler lifetime can improve gate performance. These results demonstrate the experimental feasibility of C-shunt flux-qubit couplers for combining low-interaction idling with fast entangling operations between transmon qubits.
summary: This paper reports the experimental realization of a C-shunt flux-qubit coupler connecting two transmon qubits. By tuning the coupler flux, the researchers successfully engineered an operating point that minimizes residual ZZ interaction for long idling periods while enabling fast, high-fidelity Controlled-Z gates. This demonstrates a crucial capability for building scalable quantum processors.
main_problem: The challenge is to operate superconducting quantum processors in a regime that allows for both fast entangling gates and low-error idling, as these require distinct operating conditions.
main_result: The authors experimentally demonstrated a C-shunt flux-qubit coupler enabling a 45 ns Controlled-Z (CZ) gate with a fidelity of 99.23% and confirmed an idle region with near-zero residual ZZ interaction.
method: The study employed spectroscopy, conditional Ramsey measurements, and interleaved randomized benchmarking to characterize the coupler and measure gate fidelities.
model_or_system: The system is a transmon-C-shunt-transmon (TCT) device where two transmon qubits are coupled via a flux-tunable, three-junction capacitively shunted flux-qubit coupler. The interaction is controlled by tuning the coupler flux to engineer the effective Hamiltonian.
key_observables: CZ gate fidelity (99.23%), single-qubit X-gate fidelity (>99.7%), residual ZZ interaction strength ($\zeta_{ZZ}$), and effective transverse exchange ($g_{	ext{eff}}$).
important_parameters: Coupler energy relaxation time ($T_{1,c} = 1.1 \mu$s), gate time (45 ns), and the ability to tune the system to an idle point where $\zeta_{ZZ} \approx 0$.
main_assumptions: The primary limitation identified is the coupler energy relaxation time, which is modeled using a Lindblad master equation to estimate error contributions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the TCT architecture, spectral engineering maps showing the $|g_{	ext{eff}}| - |\zeta_{	ext{ZZ}}|$ plane, and randomized benchmarking results for both single-qubit and CZ gates.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the need for tunable interaction control, details the TCT device and its Hamiltonian, presents characterization via spectroscopy and mapping the idle region, and concludes with the measurement and analysis of the fast CZ gate fidelity.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete experimental blueprint for advanced quantum gate operations by solving the conflict between gate speed and idling coherence, which is a major hurdle in scaling superconducting quantum processors.
